definition: An attack where simply visiting a web page runs code that probes the browser for flaws and, if it finds one, installs malware on the visitor's device with no file to open and often no click.
example: A trusted news site serves a malicious ad; an employee with an unpatched browser loads the page and malware quietly installs on the laptop.
category: 2.2 Threat vectors and attack surfaces > Vulnerable software
keyPoints: Delivered through compromised legitimate sites, malicious ads (malvertising) or injected scripts
Targets the client: browser, plugins, their unpatched flaws
A watering hole attack often uses a drive-by on a site the target group visits
Defenses: patch browsers, sandboxing and isolation, script and ad blocking, exploit protection
Differs from phishing: the user is only browsing, not tricked into opening something

definition: A botnet is a group of infected devices (bots) that an attacker controls remotely. The attacker sends them orders through a command and control (C2) channel, and the bots report back the same way.
example: The Mirai malware logged in to cameras and routers with default passwords, joined them to a botnet and had them flood targets with traffic on command.
category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
keyPoints: Used for DDoS, spam, credential stuffing and spreading more malware
C2 traffic tries to look normal: common ports, HTTPS, DNS, legitimate cloud services
Indicators: regular beaconing to an unknown host, odd outbound traffic, unexplained resource use
Blocking the C2 domain or address cuts the bots off from orders
IoT devices with default credentials are common recruits

definition: Taking over a user's logged-in session by stealing or guessing the session token (usually a cookie) the server uses to recognize them, so the attacker is treated as that user without needing the password.
example: Script injected through an XSS flaw reads a shopper's session cookie and sends it to the attacker, who pastes it into a browser and is inside the shopper's account.
category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Application attacks
keyPoints: Token stolen by sniffing unencrypted traffic, XSS, an on-path position or a guessable token
Bypasses MFA, since the login already happened
Defenses: HTTPS everywhere, Secure and HttpOnly cookies, random tokens, short timeouts, new token at login
Replay is the wider idea of resending captured data; hijacking takes over the live session
Indicator: the same session used from two places at once

term: Evil twin and rogue access point
definition: A rogue access point is any wireless access point connected or running without authorization. An evil twin is a rogue access point set up to imitate a legitimate network, using its name, so people connect to it and the attacker sits in the middle of their traffic.
example: In an airport, an attacker broadcasts the airport's free Wi-Fi name with a stronger signal and shows a fake login page that collects travelers' email passwords.
category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Network attacks
keyPoints: Evil twin copies the SSID and often boosts its signal or knocks clients off the real network
Leads to sniffing, credential capture through fake portals and on-path attacks
A rogue AP may be an employee's own router plugged into the office network, with no bad intent
Detect with a wireless IDS/IPS and site surveys

Defenses: 802.1X (WPA2 or WPA3 Enterprise) with server certificate checks, users heeding certificate warnings, VPN on public Wi-Fi; a shared Wi-Fi password does not stop a twin run by someone who knows it

definition: Malware that runs mainly in memory or through tools already on the system, such as PowerShell, WMI or the registry, instead of a program file on disk, so file scanning antivirus has little or nothing to inspect.
example: A macro starts PowerShell, which downloads a script straight into memory and stores a command in a WMI subscription so it runs again after every reboot.
category: 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity > Malware attacks
keyPoints: Lives off the land: abuses trusted built-in tools
Some types leave no file at all; others hide in the registry or WMI repository
Signature scanning of files misses it; behavior monitoring, memory scanning and EDR find it
Indicators: unusual PowerShell or script activity, odd parent and child processes, encoded command lines
Restarting may clear memory-only malware but not its registry or WMI persistence
